flawed_step: Step 4: the claim that a longest cycle C of a 2-connected Eulerian graph can always be extended to take in a vertex outside C does not follow. Neither even degrees nor 2-connectivity forces this, and K_{2,4} shows it can fail.
counterexample: K_{2,4}, with parts A={a1,a2} and B={b1,b2,b3,b4}. The degrees are 4,4,2,2,2,2, all even, and the graph is connected, so it is Eulerian. Deleting a1 leaves the star K_{1,4}, and deleting some b_i leaves K_{2,3}; both are connected, so the graph is 2-connected. It is bipartite with unequal parts (2 and 4). A Hamiltonian cycle would have to alternate between the parts and so would need equal parts. So the graph is not Hamiltonian.
assessment_summary:
Proof attempt:
1. Let G be a 2-connected Eulerian graph on n≥3 vertices. — Justified: this is the hypothesis.
2. G has a cycle, since a 2-connected graph has minimum degree at least 2. Take a longest cycle C. — Justified: finiteness plus minimum degree at least 2.
3. Suppose C misses some vertex v. By 2-connectivity (Menger / fan lemma), there are two paths from v to C that share only v and end at different vertices x and y of C. — Justified: standard fan lemma, since |C|≥3 and G is 2-connected.
4. Replace one arc of C between x and y with the path x–v–y. This gives a cycle longer than C, which contradicts maximality. — NOT justified: the new cycle is longer only if the arc it replaces is shorter than the detour. If x and y are adjacent on C, or all such arcs are at least as long, nothing is gained. Even degrees do not rule this out. This is where the argument fails.
5. So C is Hamiltonian. — Not justified: it depends on Step 4.

Checking whether Step 4 could be repaired: it cannot, because the statement is false. In K_{2,4} every vertex has even degree (4 or 2), the graph is connected, and deleting any single vertex leaves K_{1,4} or K_{2,3}, both connected. So it is 2-connected and Eulerian. It is also bipartite with parts of size 2 and 4. Any cycle alternates between the parts, so it uses equally many vertices from each; the longest cycle has length 4 and misses 2 vertices. Hence no Hamiltonian cycle exists. More generally, K_{2,2m} for m≥2 is a counterexample. Verdict: the statement is false.
